professional: an applied statistician of point processes who evaluates wake-word / keyword-spotting false-accept rates (false accepts per hour). evidence.craft: Read sim.py (92 lines), __init__.py, run.py, figure.py, tests/test_sim.py. Clean, vectorised numpy; the chunked AR(1) with an overflow-safe chunk length is correct (checked by the independent simulator). Defects: sim.py:80 docstring says 'windows are simulated independently' but within a 40-window group the windows are contiguous slices of one AR(1) series and the lockout state carries across window boundaries (negligible at phi=0.9, but the docstring is wrong); wake_positions misses a run that reaches m before frame m (edge case, negligible); lockout is a Python loop over wakes (fine at this rate). No dead code, no copied engine.
evidence.claims: Backed: every headline number (see completeness), the stylised/Gaussian AR(1) disclaimer, AI-assistance note, 'Fano factors ... textbook; nothing claimed as new theory', window-length result explained as a consequence of i.i.d. per-window drift. Failing: README:44 says that at the deployed rate (~1 wake a day) 'the same drift gives a Fano factor nearer 1' because variance ~ mean^2 CV^2. That treats the rate's CV as fixed, but a farther tail is more scale-sensitive (d log rate / d log scale ~ th^2). Computed (rare.py, m=1, phi 0.9, th=5.125 for 1 wake per 8.64e6 frames): sigma 0.05 gives Fano about 6.4 and mean 2.1 a day; sigma 0.10 gives Fano about 146 (vs 62 at 50 per window) and mean 9.5 a day, CV of the rate 3.9. The claim is wrong at sigma 0.10 and misleading at 0.05, and it is the bridge to the deployed case. Minor: README:34 runtime stale; sim.py:80 independence. 2.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can reuse the simulator (correct, reproducible). But the headline results are closed-form consequences: drift overdispersion is the mixed-Poisson law of total variance (Fano = F0 + Var(lambda)/E(lambda)), which my 0.5 s quadrature reproduces to within the bootstrap interval for m=1 without simulation; window-length invariance follows from i.i.d. drift by construction; the lockout result is the non-paralyzable dead-time counter (Fano -> 1/(1+rL)^2). Nearest prior work, none cited: Greenwood and Yule (1920) / negative-binomial overdispersion of mixed Poisson counts; Rice (1944-45) and Cramer-Leadbetter on level upcrossings; Feller (1948) and Muller (1973) on dead-time counters; keyword-spotting evaluation in false accepts per hour (e.g. the Hey Snips and Google KWS evaluations). The README disclaims new theory, which is honest; the result is sound for its model, not new, and the deployed-rate extrapolation it offers is wrong. 2.
evidence.domain: Compared against point-process practice (Fano factor, mixed-Poisson, dead time) and KWS false-accept evaluation. Correct: m-consecutive-frame trigger, Fano with ddof=1, percentile bootstrap over windows, bisection threshold calibration giving comparable means, unit-variance AR(1). Departures: no analytic check of the simulation against the upcrossing rate or the mixed-Poisson formula (both available and both agree); drift sigma values assumed, not measured (stated); the rare-rate extrapolation that the deployed question turns on gets the direction wrong at sigma 0.10; the lockout comparison reports burstiness reduction without noting that it is dead-time theory and that it changes the false-accept rate the threshold was calibrated to. 2.

defects.what: The rare-rate limitation is wrong: it says at ~1 wake a day the same drift gives a Fano factor nearer 1 (variance ~ mean^2 CV^2), but the rate's CV grows with the threshold (far tail more scale-sensitive). Mixed-Poisson quadrature at th=5.125 (1 wake per 8.64e6 frames, m=1, phi 0.9): sigma 0.05 Fano ~6.4, mean 2.1/day; sigma 0.10 Fano ~146 (vs 62 at 50 per window), mean 9.5/day

The drift engine behind every headline number is untested beyond 'drift > 2x base': replacing per-window drift with one scale per 40-window group doubles the m=3 sigma 0.05 Fano (9.38 -> 20.16) and all 9 tests pass; the AR(1) chunk-join carry error also survives

No prior work cited for mixed-Poisson overdispersion (Greenwood-Yule, negative binomial), level upcrossings (Rice), dead-time counters (Feller, Muller) or KWS false-accepts-per-hour evaluation; the headline results are closed-form consequences that an analytic check reproduces in 0.5 s (novelty is honestly disclaimed)
README says run.py takes about 15 minutes; it takes 189 s
Docstring says windows are simulated independently; within a 40-window group they are contiguous slices of one AR(1) series and the lockout carries across window boundaries

verdict: Every number reproduces byte for byte (189 s) and agrees with sources the author did not use: the analytic AR(1) upcrossing rate (50.28 vs 50.26 wakes per window), the mixed-Poisson law of total variance for the drift Fano factors (14.80 vs 14.48 at sigma 0.05, 65.0 vs 61.7 at 0.10, inside the bootstrap interval), and an independent plain-loop simulator for lockout and drift (32.00 vs 32.13, Fano 0.46 vs 0.47). The code is clean and the stylised model is honestly labelled. But the one step toward the deployed question is wrong: the README says at ~1 wake a day drift gives a Fano factor nearer 1, while the same calculation at that threshold gives about 146 at sigma 0.10 and a 9.5x inflated daily mean; the drift engine is untested (a seeded change that doubles the headline Fano passes all 9 tests); and the results are textbook consequences (mixed Poisson, dead time) with no prior work cited. Finished as scoped; below the bar on claims and verification, median 2.
